title: Heart failure: how the main drug classes work together
ariaLabel: Schematic of heart failure drugs: angiotensin, sympathetic activity, aldosterone, falling natriuretic peptides and kidney sodium handling all load a failing heart, and fluid builds up as congestion. ACE inhibitors, receptor blockers and ARNI act on the angiotensin system, beta-blockers on the sympathetic system, spironolactone and eplerenone on aldosterone, sacubitril on natriuretic peptide breakdown, SGLT2 inhibitors on kidney sodium and glucose, and loop diuretics on salt and water.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.

drugs.label: four drug classes together (not a prescription)

blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: RAAS activation
nodes.info: Angiotensin II raised in heart failure. The slider sets how strongly the neurohormonal systems are switched on.

nodes.label: Angiotensin effect
nodes.info: Angiotensin II drives vessel narrowing, fibrosis and salt retention.

nodes.label: Sympathetic activation
nodes.info: Chronic sympathetic over-activity in heart failure.

nodes.label: Sympathetic effect
nodes.info: Raised heart rate and long-term damage to heart cells.

nodes.label: Aldosterone
nodes.info: Aldosterone raised through angiotensin and other signals.

nodes.label: Natriuretic peptide
nodes.info: Peptides made by the stretched heart that widen vessels and make the kidney lose salt.

nodes.label: Peptide lost
nodes.info: Protective peptide that has been broken down.

nodes.label: Kidney SGLT2
nodes.info: The kidney reabsorbs filtered glucose and sodium through SGLT2.

nodes.label: Sodium kept
nodes.info: Sodium and glucose returned to the blood.

nodes.label: Salt and water retention
nodes.info: The kidney keeps salt and water when the heart pumps poorly.

nodes.label: Heart strain
nodes.info: A teaching score for the neurohormonal strain on a failing heart: remodelling, stiffening and wasted energy.

nodes.label: Congestion
nodes.info: A teaching score for fluid congestion: breathlessness, ankle swelling and fluid in the lungs.

edges.label: ACE, AT1
edges.info: ACE inhibitors stop angiotensin II being made and angiotensin receptor blockers block its receptor; sacubitril with valsartan (ARNI) blocks the receptor and also raises natriuretic peptides.

edges.label: beta receptors
edges.info: Beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) block beta-1 receptors, lowering the rate and the harmful long-term drive on the heart.

edges.label: MR receptor
edges.info: Spironolactone and eplerenone block the mineralocorticoid receptor, lowering fibrosis and salt retention.

edges.label: neprilysin
edges.info: Neprilysin breaks natriuretic peptides down. Sacubitril blocks neprilysin so more peptide survives. It is only used with an angiotensin receptor blocker, never with an ACE inhibitor.

edges.label: SGLT2
edges.info: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) increase sodium and glucose loss in urine. Their heart-failure benefit goes beyond glucose and is not fully explained.

edges.label: loop of Henle
edges.info: Loop diuretics (furosemide) block sodium and chloride reabsorption in the loop of Henle and give fast relief of congestion; they do not by themselves improve long-term outcomes.

sources: Where each class acts. ACE inhibitors, receptor blockers and ARNI act on angiotensin, beta-blockers on sympathetic drive, spironolactone and eplerenone on aldosterone, sacubitril on natriuretic peptide breakdown, SGLT2 inhibitors on kidney sodium and glucose, and loop diuretics on salt and water. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Ejection-fraction types, digoxin, ivabradine, vericiguat, hydralazine with nitrate, device therapy, doses and titration, potassium and kidney monitoring, contraindications (for example ARNI with an ACE inhibitor), outcome evidence, the mild diuretic effect of aldosterone blockers and acute decompensation care are left out. The figure does not say who should take any drug. Heart strain and congestion are teaching scores. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
